title: Oxygen loss at 200 m exceeded the solubility change in matched southern CalCOFI samples from 1984-2020
abstract: We tested whether a change in oxygen solubility accounts for oxygen loss at 200 m off southern California. We used observed CalCOFI bottles and matched 224 station-season groups at 56 stations. From 1984-2002 to 2003-2020, mean oxygen fell by 0.365 mL/L. Calculated air-equilibrium solubility fell by 0.008 mL/L. The oxygen deficit increased by 0.357 mL/L, with a conditional 95% three-year block interval of 0.236 to 0.469. Depth and gap checks kept positive deficit intervals. A shorter 1994-2020 check gave an increase of 0.169 mL/L with limits of -0.005 to 0.342, so it did not resolve a change. This extends an existing regional result with data through 2020 and explicit station-season matching. It does not identify a physical cause. Sampling changes, water-mass movement, the fixed depth and short dependent records limit inference. Code, source hashes, selected bottles, profiles, all tests and an arithmetic audit are included.

display.caption: Observed oxygen change and its exact split into solubility and negative deficit at 200 m. Bars show conditional 95% block intervals. The shorter modern-method check has an interval that includes zero.

citations.reason: Earlier regional work already found oxygen loss and higher apparent oxygen use through 2006. This is an extension, not a first discovery.
Independent Line 67 observations show that circulation and source water can affect oxygen. Our data cannot separate these processes.
